reason: Case studies with no customers behind them are invented proof. The task asks for 'realistic' narratives that demonstrate a 3x result nobody has measured, and the brief itself says the 3x and 98% figures must be confirmed before they are used. A real case study needs a named cohort, a before and after, and a customer who agreed to be quoted; that is a research task, not a writing task.

On focus: bootcamp buyers in Nigeria searching for alternatives is the acquisition audience, and the deliverable is specific enough to act on (pillar, four clusters, internal links, FAQ schema). One correction while working: drop the keyword-density targets, which no longer match how pages rank, and keep the intent and internal-link work.

Extends the same acquisition work into Kenya and Ghana, which the brief lists after Nigeria, and maps clusters to real routes rather than inventing pages. Volumes should be labelled as tool estimates with the tool named, since free keyword numbers are directional, not measured.

Store search is a real gap: the site sends people to both stores and nobody has checked what a Nigerian educator types there. The task asks for 30 keywords with a source each and a difficulty note based on the apps actually ranking, which is checkable work, and it feeds Starter sign-ups.

The Nigeria keyword and metadata work is on focus and concrete. Fix one thing before work starts: /products/ai-agents, /products/live-classes and /products/assignments do not exist on zedu.chat; the live product routes are /products/buzz, /products/channels and /products/file-management. Metadata for three pages that are not there would be wasted.

Per-student pricing is the strongest differentiator in the brief, and LinkedIn is where bootcamp founders read. One condition: 'realistic numbers' must mean numbers taken from a competitor's published pricing page with the link, or no numbers at all. An invented per-student comparison would undercut the argument.

Off the current focus. The brief is buying bootcamp and cohort-programme customers; university student clubs and GDSC chapters are free users, not buyers, and a directory of them does not help Starter to Pro conversion. It is a lot of work for a list with no buyer in it.

These are the five questions that actually stop a bootcamp director, and answering them in 100-150 words with verified features is quick, useful work for sales. Keep objection 2 honest: claim only the low-bandwidth behaviour the site or product states, not optimisations nobody has documented.

A landing page blueprint for 'virtual coding academy software Nigeria' targets a buyer the brief wants, and the structure asked for is finishable. In the copy use the site's own 'No Per-Student Pricing' rather than inventing a second phrasing like 'zero per-student penalties'.

Onboarding emails are useful for bootcamp operators and this is a small, clear deliverable. Keep the promise honest: call them first-30-days onboarding templates and leave 'boost retention' out of the copy, since the templates cannot prove a retention lift.

This overlaps T-1635 heavily: that task already maps cohort-platform keywords for Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana with intent and routes. A West Africa intent map covers two of the same countries and produces a second keyword list for the same pages. Better to extend T-1635 than run both.

Bootcamp managers comparing Zedu with Moodle, Classroom and Discord is the conversation before a switch, and the brief says Zedu replaces a mix of Slack, Zoom, Drive and LMS add-ons, so this is in scope. Every competitor claim must be checkable on that competitor's own public page, especially any pricing.
